name: Pre-workout / stim stacks
lead: Pre-workout supplements are products taken shortly before training to raise energy, focus and endurance so that lifters can train harder and longer. They are sold as powders, capsules and drinks, and "stim stacks" are high-caffeine versions, or combinations of caffeine with other stimulants, favoured by people who want a noticeable push before a session [1]. The looks payoff runs through training: more intensity and volume across a program is what lifters say drives muscle gain and a leaner, more muscular physique.

Most products are proprietary blends averaging about 18 ingredients, with caffeine, creatine and beta-alanine in nearly all of them and caffeine in about 86 percent of best sellers in one study [1]. Other common components include citrulline and arginine for "pump", taurine, tyrosine, electrolytes and plant extracts [1].

Research on caffeine is substantial: the International Society of Sports Nutrition reports small to moderate acute benefits for muscular endurance, strength, sprinting and jumping, with aerobic endurance showing the most consistent effects [2]. A review of multi-ingredient pre-workouts reports positive effects on muscular endurance and mood, with mixed results for some other outcomes and with proprietary blends complicating comparison between formulas [3]. Reviews also describe cardiovascular and sleep effects of stimulant-heavy products [4][5].

chain: Stimulants and pump ingredients raise energy and focus before training
Harder, longer or more focused sessions
More training volume and effort over time, supporting muscle growth and leanness
angle.text: Pre-workouts aim at the quality of each training session rather than at the body directly. Lifters use them to get through hard workouts, and the physique results people are after come from the extra effort accumulated across weeks of training.

paras: "Pre-workout" is a general term for bodybuilding supplements taken to improve endurance, energy and focus during training. Formulas vary by brand, and the category is lightly regulated [1]. Typical ingredients include caffeine and related stimulants (theophylline, theobromine), carbohydrates, electrolytes, nitric-oxide aids such as citrulline, arginine and beetroot nitrates, amino acids such as BCAAs, taurine and tyrosine, beta-alanine, and herbal extracts such as ginseng, ginkgo and rhodiola [1].

"Stim stack" usually means a high-stimulant combination, typically caffeine plus others such as theacrine, tyrosine or similar compounds. On looksmax.org, a member describes a product with 180 mg of caffeine as strong enough that users dance between sets [6]. On the T Nation forum, users review commercial pre-workouts, with one reporting a strong effect without jitters at one scoop and tingling at two [7], and older threads discuss timing of stimulant products and the warning labels against combining stimulants [8].

Products are sold as powders mixed with water, capsules, tablets, ready-to-drink cans and bars, and many brands offer sugar-free, creatine-free and stimulant-free versions alongside the standard high-stimulant formula.[1] Wikipedia names Pre JYM, ENGN Shred (EVLUTION Nutrition) and C4 Original (Cellucor) among top sellers in 2019.[1] Beta-alanine appears in about 87 percent of leading formulas, and its tingling is a well-known sensation that users sometimes treat as a sign the product is working.[1]

Dan Duchaine formulated Ultimate Orange in Venice, California in 1982, described as the first pre-workout and widely used by bodybuilders [1]. Ephedra-based stimulants linked with hypertension, stroke, seizure and heart attack were banned by the FDA in dietary supplements in 2004, creatine grew in popularity, and "pump" products with arginine and citrulline emerged in the early 2000s [1].

In 2005 chemist Patrick Arnold formulated a product containing DMAA, and Jack3d became a notorious high-potency brand linked to chest pain and heart risks before the FDA banned DMAA in 2012. Replacement stimulants such as DMBA, octodrine and DEPEA followed, and prohormones such as DHEA and CDMA were banned in 2014 [1]. The industry was valued at $2.7 billion in 2008 and $14.2 billion in 2022 [1].

The stimulant that anchored late-2000s products, DMAA (methylhexanamine), was originally developed by Eli Lilly as an inhaled nasal decongestant in the 1940s and withdrawn, with its drug application withdrawn in 1983. Arnold reintroduced it in 2006 as a supplement stimulant after ephedrine was banned in 2005.[17] The FDA said in April 2013 that DMAA was potentially dangerous and not a legal dietary supplement, and an appeal court upheld that position against a manufacturer in 2019.[17] Replacement stimulants such as DMBA, octodrine and DEPEA followed, prompting further regulatory attention to unapproved ingredients.[1]

The ISSN position stand reports that caffeine improves exercise performance in many but not all studies, with doses of about 3 to 6 mg per kg body mass shown to work consistently, a minimal effective dose possibly near 2 mg/kg, and side effects more frequent at very high doses (9 mg/kg) [2]. Caffeine acts as an adenosine receptor antagonist and is linked with better alertness and faster reaction time [1].

A cross-over trial compared a multi-ingredient pre-workout (beta-alanine, citrulline malate, arginine alpha-ketoglutarate, taurine, tyrosine, caffeine) with caffeine alone on bench press performance [9]. A 2025 randomised trial in middle-aged adults compared multi-ingredient pre-workouts with carbohydrate alone for resistance-training outcomes [10]. A randomised trial of citrulline malate found no improvement in muscle recovery after resistance exercise in untrained young men [11].

Wikipedia notes that reported energy effects are largely subjective, carbohydrate effects are inconsistent, and commercial doses of ingredients such as BCAAs and arginine are often below studied levels [1].

Caffeine is the base of nearly every stim stack. Wikipedia describes it as a proven ergogenic aid, with moderate intakes improving sprint times, time-trial performance, endurance and power output in humans, and possibly increasing fat oxidation during aerobic exercise.[18] Stacks add other stimulants or stimulant-adjacent ingredients to caffeine, including theacrine, tyrosine, synephrine, yohimbine and higenamine, with the intention of a stronger or longer-lasting effect.[1][16]

Stimulant-free versions keep pump, buffering and hydration ingredients, such as citrulline and beta-alanine, for users who train late or are sensitive to caffeine. Some lifters combine a commercial pre-workout with extra caffeine, coffee or energy drinks; forum threads discuss when to take stimulants and the warning labels about combining them.[8] The International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand reports that side effects become more frequent at very high caffeine intakes.[2]

Beta-alanine causes temporary, dose-dependent tingling, and nausea and skin irritation are also reported. Caffeine can raise blood pressure, and higher doses may increase cardiac and liver risks; synephrine has been linked to heart problems [1]. A 2025 integrative review of 24 studies on pre-workouts and cardiovascular health reported possible cardiovascular changes classed as adverse or cardioprotective and described the literature as limited and conflicting [4]. A case report describes pancreatitis attributed to pre-workout use [12].

A meta-analysis of 24 studies found that caffeine reduced total sleep time by about 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7 percent, and estimated that a standard pre-workout serving of 217.5 mg should be taken at least 13.2 hours before bedtime to avoid the reduction in total sleep time [5]. Sleep is also a recovery factor for muscle gain.

The FDA has minimal pre-market control over supplements, and quality studies report mislabelled contents. One study found melamine contamination in up to 50 percent of analysed pre-workout blends, and prohormones and SARMs are sometimes present undeclared, a frequent cause of failed athlete drug tests [1]. A review of selected food-supplement ingredients discusses risks of several common components [13].

Wikipedia's caffeine article reports that mild anxiety, jitteriness and insomnia are common, that doses above roughly 300 to 400 mg can cause or worsen anxiety, and that health bodies such as Health Canada and the European Food Safety Authority cite about 400 mg a day as a limit for healthy adults. It also notes that powdered caffeine is hazardous because a small quantity can be dangerous.[18] The US Food and Drug Administration, as described on Wikipedia, can monitor reported adverse events after sale but cannot test supplements before they reach the market, and many companies use third-party labs to verify ingredients.[1]

DMAA illustrates the regulatory side: Wikipedia reports that the FDA said it can narrow blood vessels and raise blood pressure, that at least five deaths have been associated with DMAA supplements, that the UK regulator ruled Jack3d an unlicensed medicine in 2012, and that the US military recalled DMAA products from its exchange stores in 2010. The coroner for a runner who died at the 2012 London Marathon said DMAA was probably an important factor.[17]

Human studies cover caffeine [2], multi-ingredient pre-workout blends on bench press, basketball performance, anaerobic performance and resistance-training adaptation [9][10][14][15], theacrine [16], citrulline malate [11] and cardiovascular effects [4]. A review of multi-ingredient pre-workouts summarises positive effects on muscular endurance and mood, mixed effects on strength and power outcomes, and the difficulty of comparing proprietary blends [3]. No study has examined high-stimulant stacks as an appearance intervention.

Pre-workout use is closely tied to gym culture: the product is part of a training ritual for people building muscle or leanness, and brand names, flavours and the tingle of beta-alanine are common conversation topics. On looksmax.org a member writes that 180 mg of caffeine is enough that users dance between sets, illustrating how stimulant strength is discussed.[6] T Nation threads review commercial products and ask about timing relative to workouts.[7][8]

The industry is large: Wikipedia cites a value of $2.7 billion in 2008 and $14.2 billion in 2022.[1] Wikipedia also reports a study finding melamine contamination in up to half of analysed blends and that undeclared prohormones and SARMs have caused athletes to fail drug tests, which is why many athletes in tested sports look for third-party-certified products.[1] Related practices include creatine, caffeine tablets, energy drinks, nitrate supplementation and intra-workout carbohydrate drinks.

timeline.event: DMAA introduced by Eli Lilly as a nasal decongestant, per Wikipedia.[17]
Dan Duchaine formulates Ultimate Orange, described as the first pre-workout [1].
FDA bans ephedra in US dietary supplements [1].
Patrick Arnold formulates a DMAA pre-workout; Jack3d follows [1].
FDA says DMAA is not a legal dietary supplement.[17]
Prohormones such as DHEA and CDMA are formally banned [1].
US appeals court rules DMAA cannot be marketed as a supplement.[17]

lore.intro: Gym-focused forums discuss pre-workouts as a way to get energy and aggression for training, and members compare products and stimulant strengths [6][7][8].

claims.claim: High-caffeine pre-workouts produce a strong training boost.
claims.believers: Users describe strong effects from stimulant products, one saying 180 mg of caffeine made users energetic between sets and another saying a commercial product was strong without jitters [6][7].
claims.experts: The ISSN position stand reports small to moderate acute benefits of caffeine for endurance, strength and sprint outcomes in many but not all studies [2].

claims.believers: Users favour blends with pump ingredients and amino acids [7].
claims.experts: Comparisons of blends versus caffeine or carbohydrate alone exist, but proprietary formulas make comparison difficult and results are mixed [3][9][10].

claims.claim: Stimulants can be combined or stacked for greater effect.
claims.believers: T Nation threads discuss pairing stimulants with other products and whether to take them together [8].
claims.experts: Product warning labels and reviews note blood pressure and cardiovascular effects of stimulant combinations [4][8].

claims.claim: Late-day pre-workout does not matter for recovery.
claims.believers: Users train at all hours with stimulants.
claims.experts: A meta-analysis found caffeine reduced total sleep time and deep sleep, with a pre-workout serving best taken more than 13 hours before bed [5].

claims.claim: Beta-alanine tingling means the product is working.
claims.believers: Users describe the tingle at higher servings as part of the effect.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes beta-alanine tingling as harmless and dose-dependent, a sensation rather than a performance measure.[1]

claims.claim: Stronger stimulants like DMAA gave better workouts.
claims.believers: Older brands such as Jack3d gained a reputation for potency.[17]
claims.experts: The FDA said DMAA is potentially dangerous and not a legal supplement; Wikipedia reports at least five associated deaths and sports bans.[17]

claims.claim: Proprietary blends contain what the label says.
claims.believers: Brands market complex formulas with many ingredients.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that commercial doses are often below studied levels and that one study found melamine in up to 50 percent of blends.[1]

card.summary: High-caffeine pre-workout blends for gym energy, with mixed evidence beyond caffeine.
card.note: High stimulant loads can raise blood pressure; contamination has been reported.

quick.overview:
Pre-workouts are stimulant-heavy supplements taken before training, mostly built on caffeine.

Caffeine has research support for focus and endurance, while evidence for many other ingredients is mixed.
quick.mechanism: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, reducing perceived fatigue and pain; other ingredients target blood flow and muscle buffering.
quick.risks: Reported risks include raised blood pressure, nausea, contamination and undeclared banned substances. The FDA has limited pre-market oversight of supplements.
